title: Accelerating inverse materials design using generative diffusion models with reinforcement learning - Nature Machine Intelligence
byline: Chen; Junwu; Guo; Jeff; Fako; Edvin; Schwaller; Philippe
html:
Abstract

Diffusion models promise to accelerate materials design by directly generating novel structures with desired properties, but existing approaches such as conditional generation typically require expensive and substantial labelled data (>10,000) and lack adaptability. Here we present MatInvent, a general and efficient reinforcement learning workflow that optimizes diffusion models for goal-directed crystal generation. By formulating equivariant denoising as a multistep decision-making problem, MatInvent leverages policy gradient with reward-weighted Kullback–Leibler regularization, including experience replay and diversity filters to enhance optimization efficiency and sample diversity. For single-objective designs, MatInvent rapidly converges to target values within 60 iterations (~1,000 property evaluations) across electronic, magnetic, mechanical, thermal and physicochemical properties. Furthermore, MatInvent achieves robust optimization in design tasks with multiple conflicting properties, successfully proposing low-supply-chain-risk magnets and high-κ dielectrics. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, MatInvent exhibits comparable or superior generation performance under specified property constraints while markedly reducing the demand for property computation. Compatible with diverse diffusion model architectures and property constraints, MatInvent could offer broad applicability in materials discovery.

Main

The development of novel functional materials is pivotal for accelerating scientific progress in various fields such as catalysis, microelectronics and renewable energy1,2,3. The key objective is to identify property-optimal candidates within an enormous design space. Existing methods include iterative experimental trial and error4,5 and high-throughput screening6,7. However, the brute-force screening of all possible materials is prohibitive, a challenge circumvented through expert-defined search spaces. Although this approach has offered success in discovering novel materials, manually constraining the search space could introduce negative bias.

Recently, generative models8,9,10,11,12, particularly diffusion models13,14,15,16,17, have emerged as promising frameworks for generating novel and theoretically stable inorganic crystal structures spanning the entire periodic table. Several methods, such as conditional generation by classifier-free guidance14, have been proposed to steer diffusion models towards generating materials with targeted properties18,19,20. Nevertheless, these methods require substantial pre-existing labelled data for model fine-tuning, limiting their generalizability and flexibility across diverse inverse design tasks.

Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a framework for optimizing generative models by iterative exploration of complex problem spaces on the basis of feedback rewards, with potential to improve generation quality and controllability21,22,23. This approach decouples learning from dense annotations by leveraging sparse or indirect reward signals, requiring substantially fewer labelled data compared with supervised fine-tuning22,23. Notably, RL has become a mainstream strategy for optimizing Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES)-based language models to accomplish goal-directed molecular generation24,25,26,27,28. The previous RL approaches for crystals focus on structure prediction of a given composition29,30 or composition generation within a narrow chemical space31, neither of which addresses de novo generation of complete three-dimensional (3D) crystal structures with target properties. Concurrent works32,33,34,35 also explore RL for crystal generation, yet lack a general framework compatible with diverse diffusion model architectures and materials properties. Furthermore, few studies have investigated key techniques for improving optimization efficiency and sample diversity in RL fine-tuning of crystal generative models.

This work proposes MatInvent, a versatile and efficient RL workflow for optimizing pretrained diffusion models towards objective-driven crystal generation. By framing denoising generation as a multistep decision-making problem, MatInvent leverages policy optimization with reward-weighted Kullback–Leibler (KL) regularization, including experience replay and diversity filters to enhance sample efficiency and diversity. For single-objective optimization, MatInvent demonstrates remarkable performance and flexibility across various materials design tasks encompassing electronic, magnetic, mechanical, physicochemical, thermal and synthesizability properties. Compared with the conditional generation of MatterGen, our RL approach substantially reduces the requirement for labelled data while exhibiting enhanced generative performance under target property constraints. Furthermore, MatInvent achieves robust optimization in design tasks with multiple competing objectives, successfully designing magnets with low supply-chain risk and high-κ (dielectric constant) gate dielectrics. This versatility makes our approach highly appealing to researchers in materials science, chemistry and catalysis.

Results

RL pipeline

MatInvent is an RL workflow designed for goal-directed generation of crystalline materials (Fig. 1). In the pipeline, the diffusion model acts as the RL agent that generates novel 3D crystal structures through a T-step reverse denoising process on atomic types, atomic coordinates and lattice matrices13,14. The denoising process of the diffusion model can be reframed as a T-step Markov decision process (MDP)22,23 for our online RL algorithms (Methods). We denote the diffusion model before RL fine-tuning, which was pretrained on large-scale unlabelled datasets of crystal structures (for example, Alex-MP14) and can generate diverse crystalline materials spanning over 80 elements, as the prior. In each RL iteration, the diffusion model randomly generates a batch of m crystal structures. The generated structures undergo geometry optimization using universal machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs)36 and their energy above hull (Ehull) is calculated. Only crystal structures that are thermodynamically stable (Ehull < 0.1 eV per atom), unique and novel (SUN)14 are retained after filtering, in which n samples are randomly selected for property evaluation and assigned corresponding rewards. The materials properties and rewards can be obtained through theoretical simulations, ML predictions and empirical calculations. The top k samples ranked by reward are used to fine-tune the diffusion model on the basis of policy optimization with reward-weighted KL regularization (Methods). The KL regularizer between the pretrained and fine-tuned models is incorporated into the RL objective function to prevent reward overfitting while preserving the materials knowledge acquired during pretraining22. Moreover, experience replay and the diversity filter are respectively employed to improve optimization efficiency and sample diversity of the RL process, enabling faster convergence towards the target while generating novel and diverse crystal structures. Experience replay is used to improve the stability and efficiency of learning by storing past high-reward crystals in a replay buffer and reusing them during RL fine-tuning27,37. The diversity filter imposes a linear penalty on the reward of non-unique crystal structures on the basis of the number of previous occurrences38,39. Specifically, crystals with the same structure or composition as previously generated samples are assigned reduced rewards and subsequently removed from the replay buffer, thereby encouraging the diffusion model to explore unseen materials space. Notably, MatInvent is a general-purpose RL workflow that is compatible with different diffusion model architectures (Supplementary Section C.1). Unless otherwise specified, all experiments in this work use the MatterGen14 framework as the diffusion model in the RL process.

a, A schematic overview of MatInvent methodology. In each RL iteration, the diffusion model acts as the RL agent to generate a batch of 3D crystal structures, which are subsequently geometrically optimized using machine learning potentials. Only valid SUN structures are retained after filtering, proceeding to target property evaluation and reward assignment. High-reward samples are then used to fine-tune the diffusion model by policy optimization with reward-weighted KL regularization, aided by experience replay and a diversity filter to enhance sample efficiency and diversity. b, The impact of geometry optimization (opt) and SUN filtering before property evaluation on the SUN ratio of generated structures during the RL process targeting a density of 18.0 g cm−3. c, The effect of experience replay on the optimization efficiency of the RL process targeting a density of 18.0 g cm−3. d, The role of the diversity filter in the composition diversity of generated structures during the RL process with a target density of 18.0 g cm−3.

To investigate the importance of individual components in our RL workflow, ablation studies were conducted using the materials design task with a target density of 18.0 g cm−3 (Supplementary Section C.2). Two metrics, the SUN ratio and composition diversity ratio, are defined to evaluate the generation quality and diversity of materials structures from diffusion models (Supplementary Section B). As shown in Fig. 1b and Supplementary Section C.2.1, MLIP-based geometry optimization and SUN filtering before property evaluation improve both the SUN ratio and composition diversity of the generated structures during the RL process. As depicted in Fig. 1c and Supplementary Section C.2.2, experience replay enhances the RL optimization efficiency, enabling faster convergence to the target property value with fewer property evaluations. This is particularly important for materials properties that have expensive evaluation costs. Moreover, the diversity filter can encourage diffusion models to explore different chemical systems and achieve a higher diversity ratio of chemical compositions during the RL process (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Section C.2.3). This facilitates the design of diverse crystal structures with target properties and prevents the RL optimization from stagnating in local minima.

Single-property optimization

In numerous applications, such as energy storage, superconductivity and electronic devices, the primary demand lies in designing novel materials with targeted or enhanced properties. MatInvent was evaluated on different inverse design tasks for single-property optimization. These tasks encompass various properties of inorganic materials, including electronic, magnetic, mechanical, thermal, physicochemical and synthesizability characteristics. The property values and corresponding rewards are derived from density functional theory (DFT) calculations (Fig. 2a,b), MLIP simulations (Fig. 2c,d) or ML prediction models (Fig. 2e–g). The first task (Fig. 2a) aims to generate materials with a target band gap of 3.0 eV, a key property for light-emitting devices40, photocatalysis41 and wide-band-gap semiconductors42. In the second task (Fig. 2b), the goal is to design materials with magnetic densities higher than 0.2 Å−3, a prerequisite for permanent magnets14. The third task (Fig. 2c) involves generating novel inorganic compounds with specific heat capacities exceeding 1.5 J g−1 K−1, which is crucial for thermal energy storage and high-temperature protection materials43. The fourth task (Fig. 2d) focuses on designing novel crystal structures with strong epitaxial matching to the commercially dominant Si(100) substrate, requiring a minimal co-incident area (MCIA) below 80 Å2 (ref. 44). A lower MCIA indicates a higher degree of matching between the thin-film material and the substrate, which is crucial for materials synthesis techniques such as chemical vapour deposition and sputtering44. The fifth task (Fig. 2e) targets the generation of materials with a high bulk modulus of 300 GPa, an essential property for superhard and aerospace materials45. The sixth task (Fig. 2f) focuses on discovering new materials with high total dielectric constants exceeding 80, important for applications such as electronic devices and supercapacitors46,47. The seventh task (Fig. 2g) investigates the generation of materials with high synthesizability scores on the basis of feedback from the ML model48, aiming to design novel and experimentally synthesizable materials. Finally, the eighth task (Fig. 2h) is to design new materials with low supply-chain risk, requiring a Herfindahl–Hirschman index (HHI) score49 below 1,250 directly computed through PyMatGen50. Further details of the RL experiments and reward calculation are provided in Supplementary Sections E.1 and E.2, while the methods for materials property evaluation are described in Supplementary Section D.

a–h, The optimization curves (left) for RL and visualizations of some generated crystal structures (right) on different design tasks with a single target property (grey dashed lines represent target values): band gap equal to 3.0 eV (a); magnetic density higher than 0.2 Å−3 (b); specific heat capacity exceeding 1.5 J g−1 K−1 (c); MCIA below 80 Å2 on the Si(100) substrate (d); bulk modulus of 300 GPa (e); total dielectric constants exceeding 80 (f); synthesizability score higher than 0.9 (g); HHI score below 1,250 (h). Curves show mean values across independent RL runs (n = 6 for c–h; n = 3 for a,b), each contributing its per-loop mean property value; shading (error band) indicates s.d. across runs.

As shown in Fig. 2, across all tasks, the average property values of the generated materials progressively approach the target values with successive RL iterations. Remarkably, within 60 iterations and ~1,000 property evaluation calls, the average property values converge to their targets for most tasks. Six more single-objective design tasks were also explored (Supplementary Section E.3), involving shear modulus, Young’s modulus, Pugh ratio, formation energy, crustal abundance and price. Moreover, the property distributions of the SUN structures generated by the RL fine-tuned model displayed a clear shift, and became more concentrated around the target values compared with the pretrained model (Supplementary Section E.4). This confirms that MatInvent can optimize diffusion models and steer their generative distribution towards regions of materials with desired properties. As depicted in Supplementary Section E.5, most RL fine-tuned models exhibited higher SUN ratios (>45%) than did the initial pretrained model (38.7%), which can be attributed to MLIP-based structure optimization and SUN filtering before property evaluation. All results demonstrate that MatInvent is an efficient and general RL framework for diffusion models in single-property inverse design tasks.

We further compared MatInvent with the state-of-the-art conditional generation method (MatterGen14), on two specific tasks: targeting materials with band gaps of 3.0 eV and magnetic densities exceeding 0.2 Å−3. For a fair comparison, all RL experiments used the same unconditional MatterGen model pretrained on the Alex-MP-20 dataset as the initial model14; more details are in Supplementary Section E.6. For MatterGen’s conditional generation, the pretrained model with adaptor modules undergoes fine-tuning on pre-existing and DFT-labelled datasets, subsequently applying classifier-free guidance to steer crystal generation towards the desired objectives14. As illustrated in Fig. 3a, MatInvent needs only 1,600 DFT calculations to obtain rewards for 100 RL iterations, substantially reducing the high DFT costs required for model fine-tuning compared with MatterGen’s conditional generation (Supplementary Section E.9). Moreover, the RL-fine-tuned model demonstrates approximately twice the SUN ratio compared with the conditional generation of MatterGen (Fig. 3b). Further details are listed in Supplementary Section E.5 regarding individual values of stability, uniqueness and novelty for unconditional MatterGen, conditional generation and MatInvent.
